utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to make an objection, because I didn't know, actually, what was happening in connection with this witness. I think this is just a pretext for a change in the order of the witnesses, and I wish to state this for the record, because the witness who was mentioned yesterday received protective measures from you only a couple of days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. We're in the middle of the examination of this witness, and as you should know by now, if a witness is giving evidence, he shouldn't be interrupted unless it's some relevant part of his evidence which is being objected to. We'll come back to that. We'll come back to that when we finish this witness, and we can then deal with the order of witnesses, the next witness, and anything else you want to raise, but let us finish this witness, your cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I had in mind that this subject was raised in the middle of the cross-examination by Mr. Nice. So I thought I was entitled to finishing it. But never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. C-013, you were speaking about prisons, and as far as I understand it, you knew nothing about who was in prison the prisons, what they were doing there, what the conditions inside were. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that they existed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there Serbs and Croats in those prisons, criminals who had been arrested on various grounds because of their conflict with the law? And people of other ethnicities living in the area, they were all there, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since you didn't have anything to do with prisons, how did it happen that you released some people from prison as a result of which you say you had problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this matter was discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we turn to Exhibit 375, tab 1, the first letter. And for the purposes of this questioning, if you turn to page 8 of the English statement of the witness, middle paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: C-013, when you gave evidence yesterday, you told us that the man who came to see you about events at the prison and who gave you this letter then discussed the matter with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. It wasn't just one man; he was Zeljko Cizmic, the chief of the police station in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, please? You told us yesterday that he discussed the letter with you when he met you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not understand the question. Are you referring to this man that I mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am referring to this man.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you explain why in your statement, when you referred to this man coming to your office and giving you this letter to be handed to the minister, you said, "Without telling me anything about the contents of the envelope, he left my office"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know what was in the envelope, that is true, just then. But then we had a short conversation. Something had happened. Such-and-such a person was there, and then he left the office, and they did such-and-such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If that is your answer, can you also explain, then, why in your statement you have said: "Finally I opened it, and found a document inside. "Having read the document, I realised that it referred to a very serious incident." And that reading of the document was sometime later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you explain the difference in your stories to this Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days ago, I explained that this, this document, was made four years ago, and that after coming here, many things came to mind, and I wanted to complement many points, and maybe that is the difference, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at this document, which I think you mean the statement, that was made during a period of two days, the 16th and 17th of May of 1999. That was closer --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to the time of these events. Isn't that more likely to be a more accurate representation of what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any major differences between the two stories. That is what happened. Now, whether that person said anything to me just then or not, and then I later remembered, I think that is not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, that's for others to judge. But I'm giving you an opportunity to explain it because this document and what it means has been challenged by the accused. Do you understand? And it's to be tested as to whether you're telling the truth or not. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, this statement goes on to say - and I'm turning to page 9, Your Honours - that your discussion with the man Cizmic took place after you had opened the letter, some days later, not before receiving the letter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, that we spoke very briefly, maybe for a couple of seconds then, and then the conversation took place later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the letter which is dated the 23rd of September, do we take it that copies of this letter were sent to other places? Don't identify those places.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to letter two. This letter you said you'd never seen when you gave evidence yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know which letter you're referring to, but I had never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the letter, your evidence was that in fact you should have received a copy of it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to give us any explanation, then, as to why, if this official report was typed up for you and you were named as the first Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. person to receive it, can you give any explanation why you wouldn't have received it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot. I really cannot provide an explanation why I did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the report itself, does it say who wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who does it identify as writing the report? Can you point that out to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Zeljko Cizmic, the commander of the Dalj police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It said that he signed -- it's shown that he signed the report, but it doesn't say that he wrote the report or conducted the interview that's described within the report. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will need to explain to you the role of the police commander to be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do we need to go into private session for that or can it be public session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do it in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could, then, give a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say briefly the commander or commanders of the police do not compile such notes. This is done by the operatives whose duty it is to do that. The commander sends them into the field to establish what had been done, any incidents or acts, and then they have to report to him as to what had been done. He has the right to allow one of the operatives, or order him, to write down what has been done, and he can just sign such a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got one other matter to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For this purpose, Your Honours, if you could turn to page 5 of the statement, top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you gave evidence, C-013, you told us that you went to Belgrade and, amongst other things, collected weapons, and you gave the Court details about that and about bringing them back. Can you explain the apparent contradiction in your statement which says that at the time of collecting equipment, equipment was delivered from Serbia for the militia and you were called at home and told to come and take over the equipment, and you took the truck to the office and stored it there, and the next morning distributed it, being the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think we have to go into private session because it's now actually touching very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I would also like to refer to your statement, and it's actually the last paragraph of page 10, and I would like to quote. You say here: "I would also like to state that I have more information directly related to crimes committed in the territory of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. This information could jeopardise my life if leaked out. Therefore, I'm not willing or able to discuss it with the investigator at present." At the time when you gave that statement, were you afraid and did you, therefore, not tell all you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic suggested to you that the Serbian MUP simply assisted the SAO authorities in establishing a civilian police to prevent looting. If I understood you correctly, it was the TO forces and Arkan who did the looting. Did the MUP Serbia arm the TO and the people who did the looting? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the special forces that arrived with Zavisic and later on, did they ever help you to prevent looting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They worked independently. And to this day, I don't know what their field of activity was, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the military authorities and the persons like Zavisic, Ante Kostic, Badza, did they ever assist you in your civilian duties and prevent the looting? Effectively assist you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say quite frankly no, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned -- or, rather, Mr. Milosevic addressed with you the person Dokmanovic, and you mentioned that he visited Mr. Milosevic in April and May and that he told you that. When -- which year do you mean, and when did Mr. Dokmanovic tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year was 1991, and I saw Dokmanovic many times at TO meetings, in April, May, June. And every time he would say where he had been, what he had been doing, as well as the objectives in that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned also the person Taska when you were asked, that he went to see Milosevic. Did Taska tell you that himself or how do you know that, and about what time period are we talking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about that same time period, the same one that Dokmanovic is mentioned in except - and I have to correct myself there - this was in April and May because, as you know, I left Bobota towards the end of May or mid-May. At that time already, Tasak had been going to Belgrade every few days and he would return from there and say that he had been to see Mr. Milosevic, he had been with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you fled the region, and you actually said that you were expelled, and I would like to try to establish what you mean when you used that term. Did you leave the region because you were afraid to get killed or harmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You put it very correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You had actually a similar exchange with Mr. Milosevic in relation to the fate of the Croatian population in and around Dalj when Mr. Milosevic put to you that the Croat population were not expelled but simply withdrew. You disagreed with him, and you said that there were many instances when members of the TO entered people's houses and forced them out. Let me, therefore, clarify. Were -- was the Croatian population forcefully --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the cross-examination, I put it to the witness -- I put his own statement to the witness in which it says quite literally - and I can find the passage and read it out to you - that the Croats who remained in Dalj after the liberation of Dalj did not have any problems. And I asked him to confirm that. And then he changed his testimony afterwards. So I didn't present this assertion; I was quoting from his own statement, his own words when he said that the Croatian population over there had no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can find the witness statement and we can look at the passage. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Found it. Here it is. Page 5, paragraph 2. It says here, and this is what I quoted: "The Croats who remained in the village at that time had no serious problems." And that is quite contradictory to his answer and response to the question during the examination-in-chief the day before yesterday as to whether all the Croats had left Dalj, and in answer to that, he said all of them did, that they had been expelled from Dalj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have made your point. You've made your point. Yes. We will find it. We will look at the statement. It will be for us to make a decision about the effect of it. Now, counsel is entitled to clarify the position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection was that the lady over there was questioning the witness wrongly and presenting his assertions as being my assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've heard what you've said. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think there is something wrong with my microphone. It doesn't work. Oh, now it's working. Your Honour, I did not misquote the accused. Actually, it is -- what he put to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not spend too much time on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that Croats were forced out of their houses. Who did that, and in what kind of an amount did that take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done by the members of the TO. They were the ones who did that, and the citizens themselves, amongst themselves. And I remember very well having said that in my first statement. Neighbours against neighbours. And I also remember full well that I said that that same evening this was shown on television. So there is video footage and evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did that happen during or after the attack or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, after. This took place in the afternoon and the evening of that same day. And the camera crew had already arrived from the other side of the Danube, and this was directly televised.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic put to you this quote in your statement, that the Croats that stayed did not have serious problems. And if it is -- the complete quote is, "at that time." And I would like to ask you: At the same time you told us about the detention of people, you told us about abductions by Arkan, and you spoke about the looting. Can you explain this discrepancy as it seems, the seemingly -- this sentence, can you explain this sentence, what you meant, that the Croats that remained did not have serious problems at that time? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained -- actually, I asked him whether it was yesterday or the day before, but I explained the term "at that time," and that "at that time" meant during that particular day or two days, while the attack was going on and immediately after the attack, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the Croatian population, did they experience problems later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that too. The Croatian population, in general, is considered to be -- that is to say, the members of all the nations or ethnic groups that are not of Serb religion. I said that many such people had stayed on in Dalj, Dalj mountain, and that the two or three villages that exist up there, that they were mostly populated by Hungarian inhabitants, by Hungarians, in fact. So those are the people that stayed up there and against whom this terror was exerted mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One matter to be raised -- there is one matter to be raised. If Your Honours look at the first page of the newspaper article, where it says, "Your mandate was finished after the 9th of March. Do you believe that the 9th of March was a police mistake?" I point that out in the interests of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly we will need some other evidence on the point. Are we in open session? We are. Witness C-013, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, there are a couple of preliminary matters. It seems that Mr. Kirudja has been the subject of some protective measures. After having discussed this with Mr. Kirudja during his days here in The Hague, he is not requesting any protective measures, and I would therefore ask the Chamber to amend any prior order which would have granted any protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour, the witness spent over three years in the former Yugoslavia in an official capacity and conducted many meetings and negotiations. He has brought to The Hague his notebooks from that time and has asked that they be near him should his memory fail. They are here at the front of the courtroom. I would ask that he be permitted to have -- that they be placed within his reach so he may refer to them if he needs to during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then finally, Your Honour, in preparation for Mr. Kirudja's testimony, a number of reports that he authored were reviewed. Now, while these documents are not Rule 68 as to Mr. Kirudja, they have nothing to do with his credibility, there is a view of these documents that they would corroborate some of the statements made by the accused that might be considered in the nature of a defence. Clearance has just been received for these documents. They have been disclosed this morning. I raise this now - it's a rather small packet of documents - but just to draw the attention of the accused and the amici to these documents. They may wish to review them over the weekend, and they may wish to -- Mr. Kirudja would be the person best able to authenticate and speak to these documents, they may wish to ask Mr. Kirudja about these reports. I would also note that they are available to be entered into evidence. The provider has released any claim of confidentiality over the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So -- just a moment. The package is available, is it, whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was handed over this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was handed over both to the amici and to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they have them and they may review them over the weekend, and if they want to ask questions about them, this is the witness to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a clarification: They were handed to the registrar to be given to the accused. I don't know if he has physical possession of them yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But they'll be coming his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They can't hear you. They can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying -- my question was why we're in private session, but I see that in the meantime, it's been public, so there's no point in my putting that question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we're now in open session, so there is no difficulty about that. Yes. You've heard what counsel has said, that there will be some documents which will be served on you which relate to this witness which may be helpful to your case, so you should have a look at them over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start on the next witness, can I just mention a couple of administrative things that concern next week and Monday. Reminding the Chamber that the accused was already wanting to raise something about the witness list. He's been served with a witness list, I hope this morning, which identifies today's witness and the witnesses coming next week. I trust the Chamber has a list as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: C-39 won't start before Tuesday. Dr. Bosanac may be taken quite shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're dealing with that witness, we have, of course, made an order in relation to her transcript being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed so, and that's one of the reasons why she may be taken quite shortly. In any event, there really is the need for some resolution of some of the outstanding procedural issues. There's the financial argument, and it's now been fully addressed, or substantially addressed, in writing, and we would be anxious to dispose of that, were that convenient, on Monday. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not convenient on Monday. We recognise -- we recognise the -- that it is outstanding. Unless there's any very good reason, we would rather hear evidence. We have earmarked a date for it, which is a day on which we have to hear an interlocutory application, the 25th of February, and it may be convenient to have that day for legal argument and include Torkildsen as well as progress of the case into the agenda for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case only one other thing that we would have wanted possibly to raise on Monday, and that is part, in any event, of our general concerns about procedures, that we've had the first 92 bis application response from the amici, and I gather the other one's available and is going to be -- and is going to be served possibly a courtesy copy today and filed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will that be done, please, so we have it for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript one. We've done the 64 witnesses, was done and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It just hasn't made its way to me is all. Judge Kwon has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are obviously anxious to know what the real current consequences of the time limit are. First of all, we need -- we need to know whether our calculation of the number of days remaining matches yours, and of course, we need resolution of the 92 bis matter, because, for example, if 92 bis witnesses are all going to be cross-examined, that's another 17 days for Croatia alone on the basis of the number of witnesses we are calling, or something like that. And we need resolution of that to budget remaining time and/or to persuade the Chamber further about procedural steps that may save time. So we are very anxious that that matter can be heard as swiftly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. As I say, the date we have in mind is the 25th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help me on one thing, Mr. Nice. I'm looking at the overall number of witnesses. We had a list on the 31st of July. I take it that that has now been bypassed by the list which you provided on the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the up-to-date list from which we should be working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly the up-to-date list as of December. I can't, I'm afraid, recall whether there have been further amendments, but there may well have been. But no, that's the list to be working off for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And one chart was provided in some detail for Croatia. There's another chart that's either been prepared or soon to be prepared for Bosnia and will be served on you if it hasn't been already. I can't remember the position on that. There will be another motion about that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It would help us to know if there were any legal issues that would be taken on Monday because, if possible, I'm struggling with the judicial notice motion at the moment, which is quite a considerable document, and it's easier for me not to be in court, to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, are there any immediate issues which you need dealing with? I mean, I doubt we'll be in a position to deal with the Rule 92 bis. There are 64 at least, if not 70, statements involved and I doubt we will be able to deal with that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- if this witness takes a significant amount of Monday, as he may well now do, given the time, and if Dr. Bosanac is available, we can easily fill up Monday. But I wouldn't want -- I wouldn't want any delay to occur in relation to 92 bis because we really do need to know as soon as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The only thing is we need a date -- to fix a date to hear legal argument about 92 bis. At the moment, we have in mind the 25th of February, but if you would wish us to deal with the matter earlier, of course we'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll revert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could let Mr. Kay know when you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. But I'm sure he can safely be out of court, on the present basis, on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would the Court forgive me if I just leave and make certain arrangements which need to be made, and I'll rejoin the court after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to make an objection. In my opinion, the other side is intentionally complicating and causing confusion with the schedule of witnesses. They keep changing the order of witnesses, and you saw yesterday that the witness that should have appeared today has been removed from the list with the explanation that somebody threatened him, though it was a witness who has given, granted protective measures by you a couple of days ago. So it appears that throughout this time while he was not protected, nobody threatened him, but only a couple of days when he was granted protective measures --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suspect this is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- suddenly he was threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- oblique attempt by this witness [sic] to identify yet another witness, and we dealt with it yesterday. We dealt with it on the basis that the witness was carefully not being identified. The accused knows perfectly well what is afoot. When he said yesterday his only desire was to know the order of witnesses, I was tempted to reply that it was to do with the order of witnesses that threats were effective. I can see no substance in what the accused is raising. All that's happened is there has been some acceleration of witnesses. He is no doubt ready to deal with this witness and what he is doing would seem to me to be probably devious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We disagree. He's entitled to make his objection. Now, you know quite well that if there's anything that should lead us into private session, Mr. Milosevic, we should go in there, but we'll let you make your objection, although so far, I can see no substance in it. Now, what is it, the objection you want to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is that I believe that this is fabricated and also the next witness, Graham Blewitt, as far as I know, he's a Deputy Prosecutor, and he was not protected, and I assume that he was threatened and that's why he's been removed as well. So we have the next witness now in order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is absolutely no substance in that suggestion. If there was any question of our thinking that this list was being manipulated for some improper purpose, we would rule on it. But there is none. This is a long and complex case involving a large number of witnesses who -- most of whom come from the region or from other areas of the world. It has been complicated by the fact that you have been ill from time to time and, therefore, the time has been broken up. There is no substance in what you say. We will protect your interests, which is this: That you should have time properly to prepare for each witness. We will do that and ensure that you do. Apart from that, there is nothing in what you say. Now, let us get on with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, quickly. Quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly. I'm saving both my time and yours, as much as I can. A moment ago, Mr. Nice said that the next witness, one of the next witnesses was Vesna Bosanac, that she would be brief, with some kind of transcript being attached from an earlier hearing. I think that is also unfair, because it is directed exclusively to limit my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. In relation to a later witness, you can address us before she comes to give evidence. We're not going to waste time on it now. But if you care to look at the order which we made, you'll see that we admitted the transcript. Now, for the moment, we'll hear from this witness. In due course, we'll deal with others. Yes. No. No, Mr. Milosevic. You've taken up enough time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mr. Charles Kirudja. Your Honour, while he's being brought in, there is simply one binder of exhibits the Prosecution will seek to tender. Perhaps a number could be assigned to that now. I will be working with exhibits from the outset.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to particular take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, the Chamber has permitted you to have access to your diaries during your examination. I'd ask you to just take a moment to arrange them in a way that will allow you to get to specific dates quickly. Mr. Kirudja, who do you presently work for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I would ask you to look at this document and tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It's a copy of my resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To abbreviate your testimony, I will not ask you detailed questions about your background. Are you willing to answer questions about your educational and professional background should the amici or the accused wish to ask you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to focus in on your time in Yugoslavia. Can you please tell us what period of time did you work in Yugoslavia or the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I arrived in the former Yugoslavia first week of April, 1992, and served there until June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please briefly tell us the different locations you were stationed at during that three-year period before we continue.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: First I was assigned to Sector North and proceeded there through Sector East, arriving in Sector North Topusko around 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where did you serve next?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I remained in Topusko in the capacity position of civil affairs coordinator until around August 1994 and then was asked to relocate and resume -- and assume the role of chief civil affairs -- Chief of Staff of civil affairs in Zagreb, where I remained until towards the August 1994, and then I was posted to Belgrade in the capacity of the delegate of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, where I remained until June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to focus the first part of my questions to you on your responsibilities in Sector North. Is it true that Sector North is located in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that one of four designated areas, so designated by the Vance Plan, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that Prosecution 378, tab 2, be placed on the overhead projector, and I would point out that this is a photocopy of an earlier Prosecution Exhibit, 336, pages 20 and 21. That's the map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you recognise Prosecution 378, tab 2?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is that? What is depicted in that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It's an approximate demarcation of what became Sector North of the area of deployment of the United Nations Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did part of -- the area that you've outlined, I'd ask you to point to it with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This is the area demarcated in black, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Part of the area or the outline of Sector North, was that an internationally recognised border?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not all of it. I beg your pardon. Not all of it. The part that constituted an international border in the sense of the recognised border between Croatia and Bosnia is this part beginning right here, following that, coming right through Velika Kladusa, all of this, continuing that way, continuing that way. It proceeded the other way but the sector did not extend that far. And then this rough demarcation turns around that area, as you can see, proceeds this way, and ends there. This is not an international border.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the record captures that, would it be fair to say that the lower line on the map is the international border? The upper and the left-hand line indicates an internal border of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That's partially correct. The bottom part indicates an international border. The top part indicates an approximate extent of what became the boundary of Sector North and not necessarily an international border.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to indicate where your office was located when you worked in Sector North.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right here, in a place named Topusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that your primary responsibility in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Sector North was to work as a member of the UN in the implementation of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to please describe for the Chamber the paramount features of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Vance Plan had basically three essential or prime components which are described basically in terms of operational requirement as the first part being the complete demobilisation of the previous military forces and containment of the weapons that were issued to those units under United Nations joint custody, what in the Vance Plan is known as double key. That was the essence of the primary and immediate requirement or expectation of the Vance Plan. Second, the Vance Plan did envisage a requirement for someone to keep law and order after these forces had been demobilised. It therefore required a police force be in the area and be made up of the local police that -- be made of local police only endowed with light weapons, side weapons, and that that police be monitored closely by the UN deployment of civil police and it would be responsible for law and order, and that police be made up of representatives of the community as it used to be prior to the forces. That's the second part. Third part, the Vance Plan also envisaged that after the demobilisation, after the police is deployed in the manner I have mentioned under the monitoring of the UN, that there be conditions that would be conducive for voluntary return of all displaced persons in the area, and such conditions necessitated trying to look after rebuilding, restoration of the infrastructure and so forth, humanitarian aid and all of that, and that would be the third major component.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the second feature, that dealt with law and order. Did part of that also place restrictions on the type of governmental system that could exist in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The Vance Plan had recognised in those areas where the UN be deployed, it named opstinas - roughly translated to municipalities - that were constituted at that time, consisting of a mayor and a police force. And those opstinas named as comprising each of the sectors would be the soul recognised authority in the area for the purposes of the Vance Plan, maintenance of the status quo and law and order. An example: In Sector North, there is Vrginmost. It's a police station. It's a municipality. It had a mayor called Obradovic and it had a police chief called Djuro Skaljac. That was the recognised authority in Vrginmost. Other than that, the Vance Plan recognised the signatories of that Vance Plan, which were the authorities in Belgrade and the authorities in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So was it correct then that the Vance Plan did not recognise any umbrella governmental structure that united local municipalities in this area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, who was the head of the UN mission to Croatia at this time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Initially when this mission was deployed, it was Lieutenant General Satish Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was he a military person or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He was a lieutenant general, a military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it unusual for a UN mission to be headed by a military person?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes indeed. This was very deliberate. And the then head of the DPKO in New York, the department of peacekeeping operation, Marrack Goulding, did explain publicly why that was so, and that was because the Vance Plan was a holding pattern of the status quo pending a lasting solution, political solution being found elsewhere outside the mission, and to underscore that point, the mission was not headed as normally it would be by a Special Representative of the Secretary-General, to serve notice that it did not have responsibilities for political negotiations for the matters that separated the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, when you get to a convenient moment, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This would be convenient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, we're going to break now. In this and any other breaks there may be, may I remind you not to speak about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, just before the break you were explaining to us why a military person was the head of the implementation of the Vance Plan. I'd like to ask you a few more details about the Vance Plan. Are you familiar with the term UNPA or U-N-P-A?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It stands for the United Nations Protected Area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you please describe what was a UN protected area in terms of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Basically, these are the areas in Croatia where there had been a conflict by what was referred to in those days as local Serbs, Croatian Serbs, and that territory had been under the control of those local Serbs, and those were the areas where the United Nations protected -- protection force, UNPROFOR, was to be deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, your tenure in Sector North lasted from April 1992 until March of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what your title or titles were during that period.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: When we started out, the title was given in Sector North was chief civil affairs official, and within a few weeks, the head of civil affairs normalised that title to civil affairs coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Mr. Cedric Thornberry, director of civil affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you briefly tell us what your primary responsibilities were with respect to the implementation of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: As civil affairs coordinator, my responsibilities included seeing to it that the assets of the United Nations deployed in the mission were put fully to use and deployed for the purposes envisaged in the Vance Plan as well as in the normal way the United Nations missions are conducted. That included, specifically, an advisory role to the military sector commander in order for him to be familiar with how the mandate of the UN is to be executed. Then there were responsibilities that were civil -- civilian in nature that were directly under my responsibilities, and that was particularly in terms of civil -- work of the civil police and humanitarian work, the construction of infrastructure, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your work on the military side of this, did that include participating in negotiations regarding cease-fires, the handing over of weapons, the control of borders, and securing of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, they did include that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of your meetings and negotiations in this regard, can you briefly tell us the types of and the level of military people that you would deal with.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There were -- you could group those military groups in three categories. We have the military, our own military structure, the sector commander on the one side, that is on my team side. Then there was the military of the local forces that were there before we came in, and that divided into two groups; on the Serb side and on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the forces that represented the United Nations, what was the name given to those troops?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Those troops were always known as United Nations protection -- peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were they also known as UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes; United Nations Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the general on the Serb side who you most had contact with.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: At the beginning when we arrived in Sector North, we had to deal with the commander of the 10th Corps, Lieutenant General Spiro Nikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your duties regarding the police structures, would you be dealing with the local police chief, such as Mr. Skaljac who you testified to already?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. On the police chief -- it's not just that but all police chiefs in the opstinas that were part of Sector North, and there were a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your negotiations, or did you have any business to conduct with the member of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did the Vance Plan envisage that the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Interior had any role to plan in the implementation of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not in that area that I designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall the day that you first arrived in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that it was on or about 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you arrived, was there a UN presence in Sector North already?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, we had already two battalions deployed there; the Polish battalion and the Danish battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there a period of time when you were in Sector North that you yourself were dependent upon the JNA for fuel, food, and logistical support?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Very much in that very early period when we arrived. Not all the contingent or the means of the -- assets of the United Nations had arrived, and therefore, we depended very much so on the support of the JNA units that were still in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it not a fact that the JNA brought you to Sector North your first time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. The bus that took me from Belgrade was operated and secured by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you met in Sector North your very first day.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Other than the sector commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The sector commander, can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. It was Brigadier General Musa Bamaiyi of Nigeria.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you meet the local UN police chief?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There was the local UN police chief by the name of Kai Vittrup of Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you meet anybody else that day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a man that introduced himself to me as court liaison with the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. He introduced himself as Slobodan Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your first meeting or interaction with Mr. Lazarevic, did he offer to introduce you to someone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. He offered to -- first he offered to tell me who was who in terms of local authorities and then zeroed with one person. He said, "You need to meet this gentleman as soon as you can. He's useful or influential," whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recall the name that he told you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A man he named as Toso Paic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that Prosecution Exhibit 378 tab 3 be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I would ask you, do you recognise what is now on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Those are photographs of some of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are those some of the individuals that you've mentioned here today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who labelled this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you do that yesterday or the day before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during your tenure in Sector North, did you have other dealings with Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the context and give us, in a very summary fashion, your impression of and your interaction with Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: My initial encounter -- meeting with Mr. Lazarevic and subsequent events, he struck me as trying very much, without even my invitation, to tell me a lot of things that I didn't ask, many of which were in the nature of, like, "You will need me." And I got the feeling that I'm being framed for something. I'm being asked to be dependent on a man that I don't even know what he is quite after, and I began to be, frankly, suspicious.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you viewed him as obstructing your work?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It didn't take long for that to happen, and it did, and I -- the effect was serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us a concrete example of a way in which he obstructed your work.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not long, a matter of weeks, we had, of course, begun to hire our own local staff to assist in the UN mission in the normal way, and we had hired one resident of Topusko who was an interpreter. She began shortly to complain to me of Mr. Lazarevic in the manner that made her very nervous, and pretty soon things got out of hand. I was out on a mission on a normal day, and I come back to the headquarters to find she's been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us her name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: She was Miss Indira Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe -- when you returned from the mission, did you make inquiries as to why she was arrested?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Not only -- I actually went to the police station where she had been charged, and that was in Vrginmost, and I received from the chief of police charges against her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what were the charges against her, as best as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I remember them because they were rather difficult for me to appreciate since they didn't sound natural. The first charge was that she was hired by the United Nations without local authority's agreement. The second charge was also unnatural; she was a foreigner. I repeat, we hired her as a resident of Topusko. Another charge was that she was taking the UN to places without authorisation. That also didn't look natural, because as an interpreter, she just went along where the UN wanted to go. And finally, she was charged with the, quote, spreading misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What ultimately happened to Mrs. Kulenovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Well, as soon as I find that she is now under arrest and under these kind of charges, I feared that the worst to come to her. I just had her transported across the boundary to Bihac where we had an UNMO office, and she continued to work there in safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there another incident in which Mr. Lazarevic was acting as a translator that you believed he was obstructing your work?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Much later on, because he would come along with these local authorities whom he interpreted to us, and came a time when we had another meeting, and this time with another local official by the name of Spanovic. And during the course of that meeting, I got a hint from my other local interpreters that we are not getting the interpretation as the speaker was talking. And that, of course, was serious, because we relied on accurate interpretation from the speaker. As soon as I heard that, I notified the sector commander who was part of the meeting that this was happening, and we stopped the meeting altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we leave this area, one final question: Regarding the arrest of Mrs. Kulenovic, did you come to learn at some point that Mr. Lazarevic was behind her arrest?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. This arrest of a staff member of the United Nations we consider normally as a very serious matter, and I had to do something about it, and I did raise a concern over this with another official, and that course of that meeting where I was lodging our displeasure on the local officials, I learned that he was behind this, and the officials themselves, the local officials themselves, told me it's not their doing. He was the instigator

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, let's me ask Mr. Kirudja a question. Mrs. Kulenovic was at the police station when you went there, and then I think you said you had her transported.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you receive any objections to that? Were they cooperative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the question. One, I didn't need their acquiescence in that transfer, because all we did was put her in our own vehicles and transfer her across into Bihac, which is out -- which was outside their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I still don't understand. I mean, was she in the custody of the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She had temporarily -- as soon as I went there to complain, they had released her temporarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- during the time when I was making my complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I want to draw your attention now to a meeting on the 13th of May, 1992. On that day, had you arranged a meeting with Mile Paspalj, the then president of the RSK parliament?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I meant when I said I did make a complaint to some local officials on this matter. It was in that context that I met with Mile Paspalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you arrange the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it your intention to meet with Mile Paspalj alone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. For the simple reason that Mr. Slobodan Lazarevic was working with the military and civil officials in Kordun. Mr. Paspalj was a resident of Glina in an area where they did not have a jurisdiction, and I wanted a neutral person to lodge the complaint into.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anybody show up at this meeting --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- other than Mr. Paspalj?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. To my surprise, Toso Paic showed up in the meeting that took place in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you lodge your complaint with Mr. Paspalj?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I proceeded to make him understand the nature of my complaint and in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he respond to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. Mr. Toso Paic was the one who responded to me. Mr. Paspalj just listened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did Toso Paic say to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He sought, as best I remember, he sought now to allay my charges that this was a hostile act against the UN operation. He sought to reduce the gravity of that charge by saying this was a misunderstanding, that the charge about restrictions that we felt coming through them, was it intentional? It was specifically on the charge of taking UN people in areas that are not authorised by them. He said, "No. We didn't mean to obstruct your freedom of movement. We just wanted to protect you from going into areas where there are mines."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After that meeting, did Toso Paic come see you again that same day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting ended, and I returned to my office in Topusko. And now also later he showed up there, accompanied by the same chief of police who had arrested Mrs. Indira Kulenovic, Djuro Skaljac, and wanted to talk about the subject all again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you anything about Mr. Lazarevic's position or role in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Actually, he came candid. Not only that he said that Mr. Lazarevic was the one behind it, he just told me she was not guilty of any of these charges, but by then, I'd already taken her out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did he say about the role that Mr. Lazarevic had in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He said that from now on, there will be new liaison officers dealing with you as the UN. And that was an allusion to the liaison officers that I was using at the time that were attached to the JNA, and that Mr. Lazarevic himself was not representing himself as a liaison person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who did he say he was representing as a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A commander of Kordun, a second colonel, Cedo Bulat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now the name Paic is ordinarily spelled P-A-J-I-C. Did Toso Paic indicate to you that his name was spelled somewhat differently than that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. That "J" is dropped when he spelled his own name; just P-A-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were working to implement the Vance Plan, did it become clear to you that the Croatian side and the Croat-Serb side viewed the plan or had different interpretations of the plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. This came very early, and it was quite a serious problem, because Vance Plan had delineated opstina by opstina what constituted the areas we had to deploy our UN assets. The Croats interpreted that to mean if an opstina is named as part of that, then the civil boundaries of that opstina - read the municipality - constituted the edge of the area where we had our deployment, the area of the United Nations protected area. That they marked in their maps as the edge of the sector. On the Serb side, they did not read it that way. They read it wherever they had taken the conflict to and formed what they called a confrontation line, if you trace that sequence of the area where they were facing Croats troop to troop, that is the edge of the area where the UN had to deploy itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the difference between the areas, the opstina borders and the foxholes and confrontation borders, did those areas of dispute get a particular name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. The map drawn with one assumption or the other produced an area of difference that became known as the pink zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your duties, did you have frequent contact with the local Serb mayors in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, routine contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there anything common about their view or their expressions to you about what their desire was for the political structure they wanted to live under?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There was almost a unison refrain that we heard at every meeting regardless of the agenda; that the UN should understand what happened in these areas was a conflict that resulted into the separation of us Serbs from non-Serbs, and as soon as you understand that we Serbs now have to live apart from these other Serbs in one country, the better the peace will be restored in this area. And that refrain was heard time and time again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the transcript has recorded your last answer as "we Serbs now have to live apart from the other Serbs in one country." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. In one country, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was your response to when people would make this suggestion to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Hearing it, there was something that didn't quite click to me, and I said to them, "What do you mean by the same country? Right here. We are here now. Do you mean one country here or do you want to leave this area? It doesn't look like you're going to leave this area and go to one country where Serbs can all live together. There is a country called Serbia. Are you going to leave?" They said, "No, we don't mean that. We mean we want to live in one contiguous Serb area no matter where Serbs are."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during your work, were you involved in -- I'm sorry. As part of the Vance Plan, the JNA had agreed to withdraw from Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you involved in meetings and negotiations regarding the details of that withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the 29th of April, 1992. Did you have a meeting with General Nikovic regarding the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Can you please describe in substance what was said during the course of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: In that meeting, the purpose was for General Nikovic to supply the UN and the sector commander with his timetable and plans for demobilising, as requested by the Vance Plan, all the military units that were deployed in Sector North. And that was the discussion and we did get his plans, complete with his schedule, what it is he was going to withdraw, and where. We also got more than that. A kind of rationale, explanation of certain things the way he thought, that should be happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, what was his rationale for -- what you are about to say regarding his rationale. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It came prefaced with something that caught my interest very much, when he said, "You should understand there is a new reality taking shape in the former Yugoslavia." And he said something to the effect that when we are all done, there will be a new Yugoslavia containing seven countries, and he proceeded to name them. He named them pretty much in reflection of the republics that constituted the former Yugoslavia; Croatia, Slovenia, and then he said Serbia and Montenegro will be one Yugoslav, then he named the next country would be Serb Republic of Serbian Krajina, Macedonia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, without calling it anything else. He just called it Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, he went on to explain with regard to Bosnia, he expected when all is done, 80 per cent of Bosnia - those were the words he used - would be under the control of Serbs. Ninety-three per cent of what he termed Serbian Krajina will also be under the control of Serbs. Second general policy he explained was that the JNA that had hitherto had control of the military in those areas, had orders to withdraw all officials who were not native born either in Republic of Serbian Krajina or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the exception of 13 officers, he said, that will remain. All others who were born outside will have to leave the area after the demobilisation, except those who were born there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Nikovic was the commander of the 10th Corps of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had he calculated, if he were to remove these JNA soldiers, as you've described, had he calculated how many JNA soldiers would remain behind in the area to assume duties under some new or different form?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We didn't get into the number of soldiers. They got the formed units that were to remain. Not the soldiers, the formed units, fighting units. And he named at least of the units that would remain, along with the weapons that would be left behind, as Territorial Defence forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that Mr. Kirudja be shown now 378 tab 4. I ask that it be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you, Mr. Kirudja, do you recognise this list that's now before you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us what list --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It's a list of the units that were deployed in Sector North and that also were part of his command and that which were to remain after Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. demobilisation and the weapons that were to be -- the types of weapons that were to be left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask the director to zoom out a little bit so we can see the entire list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I would ask you, was this list created from notes that you had --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- in your diaries?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to describe briefly to the Chamber, what was your impression of General Nikovic regarding his integrity and his sincerity for the execution or implementation of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A very impressive man. I kind of -- he gave me the impression of a professional soldier, truly dedicated to his profession, trying to do a very clear job and trying to answer as best as he can the request that he demobilise his troops, and he meant it. He seemed very focused and meant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also believe that he was genuine in his efforts to demilitarise or collect the weapons in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Pretty much so. And he spoke almost in very -- a soldier; very definitive in what he wanted, very clear. In fact, now that you remind me, he said something during that time that I was saying the policies that he would leave behind, the words, "We intend to leave a clear and clean situation administratively."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did General Nikovic in fact leave a clear and clean situation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He intended to do that and in terms of the schedule that he supplied about what will be demobilised, when it will be demobilised and the result. He was that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anything prevent him from completing his task?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. We met him again in the process of seeing this schedule being implemented, and I believe might have been 10th of July when we met him, to be received with what to us was a bombshell news that, "I am no longer commander of the 10th Corps, I am called a retired general."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at any of your previous meetings with him, had he ever discussed with you that he had planned to retire around this time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. And it didn't really stand to reason, because the schedule itself had indicated that towards the end of May - two weeks or so remained - when all of what he had said would be completed; namely, there would have been a demobilisation, there would be a retirement of all the officers not born there, and he was from Montenegro himself, so it didn't quite add up that he is now a retired general two or three weeks before the demobilisation plan that had he announced to us was to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based on your conversation with him, did you form an impression as to whether his retirement was a voluntary act or a forced act?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was unmistakably something that he himself didn't expect. Therefore, it would come into the category that it was a premature termination of his role in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at some point the JNA did formally withdraw from Sector North. What I'd ask you to do at this stage, can you please compare or describe for the Chamber, or compare for the Chamber what the command structure -- how did the JNA exist prior to withdrawal, and what was left after they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Again focusing in Sector North, when we arrived, the JNA was organised in three command zones in that sector, and they had the names Kordun and Banja and Lika, these military operational zones; Kordun, Banja, and Lika. These operational zones existed before we arrived, and after the demobilisation, they remained again distinct operational zones. Taking, for example, Kordun, there was no change. It was commanded by Cedo Bulat before we arrived and, after demobilisation, it remained under the command of Cedo Bulat. So pretty much, other than the name JNA disappearing, the command zones and many of the individuals involved in it remained pretty much the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that by this time you were able to recognise individuals that you would have contact with that were formerly members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised many of these individuals as long as they wielded authority in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you see many of those individuals after the JNA formally withdrew?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This new force that remained after the JNA withdrew, was it significantly smaller than the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
