utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you mean smaller by the total number of soldiers in there or the structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take the first part. In terms of the number of actual troops, was it significantly reduced?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That would be difficult for me to give you a definitive answer precisely because of the question you asked earlier about demobilisation, that were supposed to be demobilised under the Vance Plan. So that would pose a problem in terms of how many numbers, because whatever numbers they were, they were supposed to be demobilised, and they were demobilised a little later, in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How about the second part in terms of size of the command structure?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, that did not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your dealings with this force that was left behind afterwards, what was the name of this force as it was represented to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They went by the same names they used to go. If it is in Kordun, it was the Kordun command. If it was in Banja, it was Banja. Banja had their headquarters in Petrinje, the command was in Petrinje. Kordun was commanded in Kordun in and around Topusko and Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How was the entire force referred to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They at certain points began to refer -- later not -- progressively became known as the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the term "Territorial Defence Force" used?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when was that used and what was it used to refer to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was used very early in the Vance Plan demobilisation because of the Serbs' intent on signalling to us the need to defend their territory and therefore they would not fulfil that requirement as quickly or as planned by Vance Plan, that requirement of demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Another witness has testified before this Chamber that this force was referred to internally as the 21st Corps. In your dealings with this force afterwards, did they ever refer to themselves to you as the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, not in this particular sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you familiar with Colonel Bulat's headquarters or commands?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he have more than one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to be in those commands as we discussed matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you be able to describe one of them as his primary headquarters or command?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was that located?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not far from our own headquarters in Topusko. In a wooded hilltop behind the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you give us some idea about how many times you were in that office?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Many, many times; I can't count.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware that in that office there were a number of special phones or hotlines?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. This one was easy for us to be drawn to our attention because general to general, meaning the sector commanders speaking to Bulat, military officials did request each other, Where can I reach you in case of emergency or something? And they say, There is a hotline. You can call me on this hotline. So I knew they had some lines called hotlines where the general commanding the troops could reach them if they wanted to reach them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge regarding where the other phone was on the other side of that hotline?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Colonel Bulat also have a headquarters in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. That's a wooded forest behind there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you visit what command centre?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what that centre was like.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was a very curious place because it's hard to even find where it is. It goes back to the Second World War, and it's underground, and this is a place they had the pleasure of showing to me and telling me even the Germans couldn't find them during the Second World War if they wanted to find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you taken in to some portion of the underground facility there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your duties and attempts to implement the Vance Plan, did you come to believe that there was a significant loophole in the design of the plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was very, very obvious and clear and a source of a lot of frustration for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please describe to the Chamber what that loophole was.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The Vance Plan essentially said, We want to have these UN protected areas free of all military fighting forces except police for the normal law and order. The local Serbs in that area saw that loophole and transformed what for all practical purposes were armed -- would be armed fighting forces in camouflage uniforms, they went about to transform them to local police forces, from the green colours of the camouflage colours of the military to the blue colours of the militia or police, painting APCs into blue colours of the police, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you say "APCs," you mean armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So are you saying that armoured personnel carriers that you saw green at one stage, you later saw the same vehicles now painted blue?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: When you say the same vehicles, you don't mean that I checked the licence plate and make sure it is the same, but if you went into an area where there used to be just a police station with no APCs, now you find they have APCs painted blue colour. That didn't come from outside. The only other place where the APCs were was in the military area. If you mean that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that the Vance Plan envisaged that local police would carry light arms.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The arms that you saw these military people turned police officers, the arms that you saw them carrying, was that in compliance with the dictates of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There is a time sequence involving your question. Yes, at certain times you saw that, but the time sequence would have been -- we would first try and have those equipment contained in the UN areas, and a certain point the Serbs took them all back and then they're in the hands of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, when was it that you were successfully able to bring the arms in and place them in a contained area under the security of the UN?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Sometime between July and August that was achieved that the weapons were laid down and put under UN control, double control with the Serbs and the UN controlling them. And they were demobilised from camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this is July or August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How long did they remain -- first let me ask you, the containment process, did that involve a system where it required two keys to unlock them; a key held by the UN and a key held by local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Correct. That's the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time -- or you've described a time when those weapons were taken out. When was that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They remained there until about January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were they taken out with the permission of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. It was as a result of the first of a number of actions taken on the other side by the Croats, and that was the action I'm referring to of re-taking of Maslenica, a bridge part joining Dalmatia. As soon as the Croats made that offensive, the Serbs went back and overran all that equipment, and they took them all out from storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you were beginning to describe for us the weapons that the police were carrying. Can you please now connect these events to that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as that happened, therefore, whether they were wearing blue uniform or not, they were carrying the long weapons clearly not allowed under the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to a particular area, the area of Bihac in Bosnia. In the course of your duties in Sector North, did you become aware of events that were occurring in Bihac, Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. And pretty early, because in the earlier questions you did understand we had to go to Bihac where we had negotiation, and that was a normal situation. Pretty much it became a source of conflict, and in that pocket we called Bihac pocket, in time, became a source of a stream of refugees escaping.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what was occurring -- when things did develop in Bihac. Can you tell us when that happened and what occurred in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: We got basically the first inkling all was not well in Bosnia pretty early in April. And in fact, it was at all times in a convoy involving General Nambiar in his first visit into the sector. He had arrived by air into Bihac, and we had a convoy to try to get him in, and that's when we started seeing roadblocks into the area unexpectedly, all over the place. Before that, there was normalcy completely. The whole area was normal. From there on, those roadblocks and the conflict between Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Muslims and the Serbs in that area began to intensify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what the situation in Bihac was in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They come in April and by May it was rather -- the first notice we got had to do with the request for assistance because Bihac also had one of the largest hospitals in the area, and people asking for help because they felt they cannot get all the supplies they needed in the hospital. The humanitarian supplies were coming short. And we got all these kind of indications that we needed help in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the predominant ethnicity of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The Bihac pocket, what we refer to as the Bihac pocket in that map that I showed, almost half of that international border was, on the opposite side of the border, was predominantly Muslim. All the way to certain part where the opstina of Dvor begins and continues on the left. So that pocket, up to a certain point, was predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when the JNA withdrew from this area, did it do anything in relation to the airport?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did it do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It was clear about 15th of May, I believe, around that time, give or take a day, the airport was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that was blown up by whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did any of the predominantly Serb areas that you were aware of, or in control of the Serbs, were you aware of any other airports in those areas being blown up by the JNA as they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. This one was the only area that I was informed by UNMOs. We had an UNMO observation point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And by "UNMOs," you mean United Nations Military Observers?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, located in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you to take a look at 378, tab 6, and ask you is this a report that you made regarding the situation in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the second page of that be placed on the overhead projector. And I would draw your attention to paragraph 2. Did you, in your report, indicate that the situation had deteriorated so much that both the ICRC and the UNHCR had ceased operations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Paragraph 2? Beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Paragraph 2. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you, in paragraph 4, report some sensational unverified claims by Serbs of atrocities committed by Muslims, and you believed that these claims were a concerted action by Serb leaders in both Croatia and Bosnia to isolate local Serbs? Did you report that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also in that report indicate that Serbs had retreated from the town of Bihac, leaving mostly Muslims behind and that the Serbs in the hills surrounding the town controlled the main road and strategic points and that in recent days before this report the town had been shelled from these vantage points?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to read what you wrote in paragraph 9 of this report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 and I quote: "Stories coming from Bihac and the surrounding Bosnia opstinas of Velika Kladusa, Cazin, Bosanski Novi and Bosanski Krupa thus paint a gloomy picture similar to the one in Sarajevo and Mostar. There are fears that behind the border, the mountains and the forest, unspeakable atrocities may be unfolding. This message is sent in the hope that an alert could be relayed to authorities with the competence to begin to address the problem before it is too late for the desperate people in the area. Such an action could begin with a relief operation for Bihac..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's sufficient, Mr. Kirudja. And what is the date of this memo or report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This report is dated 16th of -- yes. It's written there in French. 16th -- that has to be August. The front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd draw your attention to the second page of the exhibit, the first page of the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's a date at the top of that. Does that --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. 16 June. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time in your tenure --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can take back the exhibit. Thank you. Actually, I'd ask that tab 5 of Prosecution Exhibit 378 be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, during your tenure, did you become aware of certain activity occurring in Bosnia which we now call ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you specific details about specific instances, I would ask you just to describe generally what you learned and the circumstances under which you learned it.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Normally, we would go about doing what I describe as the mandate under the Vance Plan, and in so doing in that course, events would begin to surprise us, and such a surprise occurred particularly in that part where the Serbs controlled both sides of the border, meaning in the Sector North, the opstina, the mayor, and the chief of police, across the border, the international border, on the other side he was also facing another Serb municipality. Serb controlled. That's what I meant; Serb controlled, mayor, police. And that surprise came when we began to see requests -- first a trickle of people escaping and then a request from the UN which for all intents and purposes seems to want to recruit us to help them move massive numbers of people from one -- from their villages out through the sector into far away places, like Slovenia, Germany, or Austria. And that, in retrospect, looked very, very troubling then and now to us, that this was actually what we were being requested to do, help in moving massive people from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kirudja, I'd ask you to take a look at the overhead projector, and is this a chart that was made in conjunction with you and in consultation with your notebooks regarding or summarising the ethnic cleansing in Bosnia that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would ask the director to please focus on the uppermost portion of the chart.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise that summary beginning on 26 of May, from Dvor, ending on 22nd of July on top of the chart, as you referred to. I recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave that on the overhead so those of us unfamiliar with this complicated set of facts may rely on it if necessary, but I want to draw your attention to the 26th of May, 1992. Did, as part of your regular course of duties, did you visit the Croatian municipality of Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did something unusual happen during that visit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Outside the agenda that I was going to discuss, the mayor of Dvor stopped to make a request of me that sounded surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was that request?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He requested -- first he started with an announcement that he and his counterpart in the municipality of Bosanski Novi, across the border, had agreed to transport 5.000 people from Bosanski Novi to pass through Sector North to a destination they called Austria or Slovenia. So that was the announcement. The demand was, one, we in the sector should and could provide a film crew to film the transit of these people across the Serb-controlled area specifically to document that they passed through safely and did not remain in the Serb-controlled areas. The second demand was we provide through the ICRC presence and our humanitarian presence, the backing, logistical backing to make sure this event goes without any trauma with the people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the name of this mayor from Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The mayor from Dvor at that time on that specific date was Mr. Borojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you whether or not this group of 5.000 people were leaving voluntarily or were being forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Actually, to my surprise, he told me they are all leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was your response to this request?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: First, there was something unnatural and counter-intuitive about that and I told him so. I asked him, one, who are these people? He said they're all Muslims. I said but you are the mayor of Dvor, it is in part of the UN, and they are coming from another country and you understand Bosnia is a different jurisdiction, you don't have authority there yourself, and you want them to leave, and you tell me they are leaving voluntarily. That's third-hand information and it doesn't sound natural. Are they leaving their homes? Yes. How do people leave the natural comfort of their homes voluntarily? And he was stuck there because he realised that I didn't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Because we were meeting not far from his office, the next thing I know, he had run into his office and was holding the phone and said, "Here is the mayor of Bosanski Novi. If you don't believe, talk to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the name of the mayor of Bosanski Novi at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Later on, the full name became clear, not at that point. His name was Radomir Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you speak to the mayor of Bosanski Novi on the phone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. At that moment, no. I told both the mayor that I wasn't really going to do that at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I want to consult my notes because I know something was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Please do.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Remind me of that date again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, something he also said to me that stuck to my mind when I asked him, "You have no jurisdiction. You are talking to me from Dvor about Bosanski Novi. How come you're involved and why it is so?" And that's when he said to me something to the extent, "There is a new government in Bosanski Novi which is a part of --" and I quote -- "Serbian Republic of BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had you ever heard the term "Serbian Republic of BiH" before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. And not even from General Nikovic who was telling us of the new reality. He had never used that term. That's the first time I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened next? I'm sorry. Before we leave this meeting: After leaving the meeting, did you have an opportunity to reflect on it and did you draw some conclusions about what you were being asked to do?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Something I alluded to earlier. Part of the reason I wouldn't take the call from this mayor was what he was asking was of an enormous implication, and he didn't seem even to himself to be bothered by that, that he would be requesting the UN to participate in a movement of thousands of people to leave their homes somewhere. And because it was -- it carried this non-sequitor, difficult to understand thing, I felt I was -- I better be careful here because we're being recruited. It looks like somebody's trying to recruit us to join in something we normally never do. We don't create refugees, we help them. And that's what it seems like we're being recruited; to create refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I left Dvor, and the next day, the very next day, around noon, I was in my office in Topusko, and I'm told there is a delegation downstairs that wanted to see you, and that turned out to be the mayor of Bosanski Novi, accompanied by his executive council members and his chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I asked them in and they came into my office and proceeded to reprise the whole story that I had heard the day before, with greater explanation because, obviously, he had been told that I didn't seem to believe this claim that these people would be leaving voluntarily. So he set out to give me greater detail about why they were leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I summarised -- it boiled down to the Muslims, he said, didn't want to fight in anybody's army, but they wouldn't also leave to areas that were in Central Bosnia. They wanted to get out of the entire area. And it also boiled down, upon inquiry and probing from me, that the Muslims had refused to swear allegiance to this new Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and wouldn't fight. So the only reason they were leaving is because of what they called military weakness as a minority. It's at that point when I said it doesn't sound to me then they're leaving voluntarily, and then he said, and I quote, "Well, I admit they are -- there has been pressure brought to bear on them" from what he called Serbian military irregulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you write an exact quote of what he said in your diary?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For the sake of preciseness, I'd ask you to go to it and read it for us.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He said, and I quote: "I admit that the Muslims have been under pressure of armed Serbian irregulars."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to the 6th of June, 1992, did you receive a report about something that was occurring at that time in the town or the football stadium of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. As a routine in our office, a flash, what the military call a flash report, had come into our situation room and it was brought to my notice immediately, from the Danish contingent in Dvor, telling me they had observed a number of people across.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: UN observation posts, were they identifiable and well-marked posts? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. When we deploy UN observation posts and others, they are clearly identifiable from a long distance, with a flag flying on them, the blue flag. You wouldn't mistake them. They are clearly intended to be noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Danish contingent, it was observing, making its observations from where?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They were in Dvor. And if you go to where this company was located, across the river you can -- in the direction of Bosanski Novi, you can see a football field through binoculars, and the soldiers were looking through binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So these soldiers are in Croatia, looking across the river into Bosnia, into Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did they report seeing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They reported what they called a group of people being herded and moved around in a football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did they approximate the number of people in that football field?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I'm not sure I remember the exact number. They were in hundreds at that point when the flashpoint came in the football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were those people being detained in that football field?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: They said they were being detained there and some being herded into buses. And that's being detained in the football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the report indicate anything peculiar about the way the people had arranged themselves in the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. To our surprise, the report said the human beings being huddled there had formed themselves into a SOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They formed themselves into the letters SOS?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That being the universal sign for help.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Chamber is intending to break at quarter to two today, this would be a good spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will break. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We're just about to adjourn. Yes. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I understand that. My question is of a practical nature, and this is it: After Mr. Kirudja, I have received this new list of witnesses, and the next one is Vesna Bosanac. And a moment ago we heard from Mr. Nice that he's going to include some sorts of transcripts which will shorten the time, cut down the time. So I'd just like to know how long you're going to give me for cross-examination of Vesna Bosanac and what your intentions are. I have absolutely no idea how he's going to cut down the examination-in-chief, and I have already said that this is geared towards reducing my time for cross-examination, that that's what it's aimed it. So please tell me how long I'll have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will not reduce your time for cross-examination. The fact that the evidence is being given by way of transcript will be taken into account, and you will allowed a proper amount of time. You have no fear on that score. We will adjourn now. Monday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
